Naboth Refuses Ahab His Vineyard.<div eID="gen4642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4643" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3308"/><hi type="bold">1-3. Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard, which was in Jezreel--</hi>Ahab was desirous, from its contiguity to the palace, to possess it for a vegetable garden. He proposed to Naboth to give him a better in exchange, or to obtain it by purchase; but the owner declined to part with it. In persisting in his refusal, Naboth was not actuated by any feelings of disloyalty or disrespect to the king, but solely from a conscientious regard to the divine law, which, for important reasons, had prohibited the sale of a paternal inheritance [Le 25:23; Nu 36:7]; or if, through extreme poverty or debt, an assignation of it to another was unavoidable, the conveyance was made on the condition of its being redeemable at any time [Le 25:25-27]; at all events, of its reverting at the jubilee to the owner [Le 25:28]. In short, it could not be alienated from the family, and it was on this ground that Naboth (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.3">1Ki 21:3</reference>) refused to comply with the king's demand. It was not, therefore, any rudeness or disrespect that made Ahab heavy and displeased, but his sulky and pettish demeanor betrays a spirit of selfishness that could not brook to be disappointed of a favorite object, and that would have pushed him into lawless tyranny had he possessed any natural force of character. <div eID="gen4643" type="x-p"/>

By allowing her the use of his signet-ring, Ahab passively consented to Jezebel's proceeding. Being written in the king's name, it had the character of a royal mandate.<div eID="gen4648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent the letters unto the elders and to the nobles that were in his city--</hi>They were the civic authorities of Jezreel, and would, in all likelihood, be the creatures and fit tools of Jezebel. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3312"/><div sID="gen4650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3312"/><hi type="bold">9. Proclaim a fast, &c.--</hi>Those obsequious and unprincipled magistrates did according to orders. Pretending that a heavy guilt lay on one, or some unknown party, who was charged with blaspheming God and the king and that Ahab was threatening vengeance on the whole city unless the culprit were discovered and punished, they assembled the people to observe a solemn fast. Fasts were commanded on extraordinary occasions affecting the public interests of the state (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.3">2Ch 20:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.8.21">Ezr 8:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference>; 2:15; <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.5">Jon 3:5</reference>). The wicked authorities of Jezreel, by proclaiming the fast, wished to give an external appearance of justice to their proceedings and convey an impression among the people that Naboth's crime amounted to treason against the king's life.<div eID="gen4650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set Naboth on high--</hi>During a trial the panel, or accused person, was placed on a high seat, in the presence of all the court; but as the guilty person was supposed to be unknown, the setting of Naboth on high among the people must have been owing to his being among the distinguished men of the place. <div eID="gen4651" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3320"/><div sID="gen4661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3320"/><hi type="bold">27-29. Ahab ... rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly--</hi>He was not obdurate, like Jezebel. This terrible announcement made a deep impression on the king's heart, and led, for a while, to sincere repentance. Going softly, that is, barefoot, and with a pensive manner, within doors. He manifested all the external signs, conventional and natural, of the deepest sorrow. He was wretched, and so great is the mercy of God, that, in consequence of his humiliation, the threatened punishment was deferred. <chapter eID="1Kgs.21"/>
